lede: A 3-D model of the cup pack with the BAK 65E cells and the P0 board. At 100 W the pack now makes about 6.1 W of heat, half the ~12 W of the FEB design, and only 2.3 W of that is in the cells. The power stage on the board is now the main heat source. It sets how long a 100 W burst lasts and where the hot spots sit. The cells stay well inside BAK's limits in every case. Model values at 25 °C in still air, not measurements.

tiles.k: heat at 100 W out (2.3 W in the cells). Was about 12 W with the FEB cells
of full 100 W from a full pack at 25 °C, then 40 W to empty. The board and the cell derate end it at about the same time
hottest point on any can, worst case (pass-through). BAK allows 60 °C cell in discharge, 45 °C cell in charge
to charge from 5 % to 95 % from one 100 W charger. The 40 °C ramp starts trimming current after about half an hour

findings: The heat moved from the cells to the board. At 100 W out the cells make 2.27 W and the board 3.82 W. With the FEB cells it was about 6.5 W and 5.5 W. Cell resistance barely matters now: 12 or 16 mΩ instead of 14 changes the 40-minute energy by under 1 Wh.

The 100 W burst lasts about 6 minutes, and the board would end it anyway. It ends when the hottest cell NTC reaches 33 °C, heated mostly by the USB1 stage through the gap filler. The stage's own copper is only a kelvin short of the 55 °C board ramp by then. Moving the cell ramp to 40 → 44 °C hands the limit to the board ramp, so the burst only grows to 6.8 min. It does let the pack deliver 48.9 Wh in the first 40 minutes instead of 40.8 Wh, with the hottest can at 47.7 °C. Splitting 100 W over both ports (65 + 35 W) spreads the board heat and gives 7.8 min.

The cells are far from their limits. The hottest can point is 42.5 °C at 100 W, 48.0 °C in pass-through and 44.6 °C while charging, against BAK's 60 °C discharge and 45 °C charge cell limits. The 33 °C derate start is a comfort and cycle-life choice made for the FEB cells. It is now the tighter limit, not the cells.

Within a cell, the gradient comes from the board. The front cell under the busy stage (C4 for USB1) carries a hot stripe on its board-facing side, over the gap filler. That stripe runs up to 10.4 K above the cell's coolest point at 100 W and 11.8 K in pass-through. The cells make so little heat themselves that their core runs within a kelvin of their can. At 30 W the whole spread is under 3 K.

Between cells: the front pair (C1, C4) runs 5.0 K above the back pair at 100 W and 7.7 K in pass-through. The largest cell-to-cell difference in mean temperature is 6.4 K at 100 W, 9.1 K in pass-through and 2.9 K at 30 W.

The NTCs read low. An NTC at mid-length, facing the pack centre, reads up to 8.5 K below the hottest can point at 100 W and 4.5 K while charging. That is why charging stops at a 44.6 °C can stripe while the NTC still shows 41.3 °C. With the front-cell NTCs on the board-facing side, the firmware sees the real hot spot. The burst then ends sooner (3.8 min) unless the thresholds move up with it.
Everyday loads are easy. 30 W never derates: 3.0 h to empty with cans at or below 37 °C. 60 W runs at full power for 30 minutes, then settles at 40 W.

Charging: 89 min from 5 % to 95 % on one port, 85 min on two 45 W chargers. On two ports the heat is shared, so the hottest part runs 47 °C instead of 53 °C. The 40 → 45 °C ramp starts trimming current at 33 and 43 min. The spec's ~2 h estimate was too long.

Pass-through is the hottest case for the board. With a 100 W charger on USB1 and 30 W out of USB2, the board makes 4.8 W. The hottest part reaches 62 °C, the outer face over the board 54 °C, and charging is trimmed after 6 minutes. At 100 W the outer face peaks at 48 °C, so the pack is warm to hold over the board side.
filler: Use about 4.5 g of a soft, dispensable 3–3.6 W/m·K silicone gap filler, only where it is now. It goes between the board's B.Cu via zone and the two front cells, over each power stage (|y| 7–16 mm, z 27–53 mm), about 1.5 cc in all. The bond line is 2.75 mm at the cell tangent and opens to about 3.8 mm at the zone edges, so it has to be a gel or a cure-in-place filler, not a pad. A pad cannot follow the curved can.

Product for P0: Parker Chomerics THERM-A-GAP GEL 30 (3.5 W/m·K, specific gravity 3.1, one part, supplied fully cured). It needs no mixing or curing, a 10 cc syringe (65-00-GEL30-0010) covers about six packs, and it peels off cleanly if the module has to come apart during bring-up. For gift packs a two-part cure-in-place filler holds its shape better through drops: Bergquist TGF 3600 (3.6 W/m·K, 3.0 g/cc, 1:1, 15 h at room temperature, Shore 00 35) or Laird Tflex CR350S (3.6 W/m·K). Cure them at room temperature only, never 100 °C, with cells fitted. Both come in 50 cc cartridges at the smallest, which is far more than a few packs need.

What it does: it is a board-protection part. It keeps the hottest power part 4.1 K cooler at 100 W and 6.4 K cooler while charging. Without it, the board ramp ends the 100 W burst after 2 min. The catch is that its heat goes into C1 and C4, where the cell NTCs see it. Under today's 33 °C cell ramp that costs about 2.7 Wh over the first 40 minutes. That is one more reason to move the cell ramp up.

What doesn't pay off: a 6 W/m·K filler takes 2.8 K off the parts and nothing else. Filling the whole rail gap (+11.3 g) takes 5.7 K off. Beads between the front and back cells (+4.4 g) narrow the front-to-back spread by about 1 K. A pad from the parts side of the stages to the cup wall (+7.4 g) takes 2.6 K off. None of them is worth the mass against the 400 g target. Filler between the cells and the cup wall would do nothing: the cans already sit 0.15 mm from the wall. The 1.2 mm of PA12 and the still air outside are what hold the heat in. A 1.5 W/m·K filler (or a cheaper gel) costs only 1.5 K on the parts, so it is an acceptable fallback.
fillnote: The 100 W columns cover the first 40 minutes from a full pack. Charging is one port from 5 %. The baseline row is the design as specified. Mass assumes 3.1 g/cc. The filler is assumed to wet both faces fully. Voids in the bead would cost more than any change of material.
sens: The 100 W case was re-run for its first 40 minutes with one assumption changed at a time. Cell resistance hardly matters. What matters is the ambient temperature (at 35 °C the cells start inside the derate ramp, so there is no burst), where the NTCs sit, and the derate thresholds themselves.
assumptions: 25 °C, still air, pack standing alone. Every outer face loses heat at 10 W/m²K (natural convection about 4.5, radiation about 5.5 with emissivity 0.9). The pack-pocket run uses 4 W/m²K.

14 mΩ per cell at 25 °C from 30 % to 100 % charge, rising to 1.8× at empty and falling about 27 % by 45 °C. BAK only gives ≤ 8 mΩ at 1 kHz. A single-cell check reproduces BatteryRealData's 25 A test peaking at 80 °C with 14–16 mΩ, and the 12 and 16 mΩ runs bracket it.
Not modelled. At these currents it can be a real fraction of the cell heat, but the cells make only about a third of the pack's heat. It moves cell temperatures by about a kelvin.

68 J/K per cell (72 g at 0.95 J/g·K). The wound roll conducts 0.6 W/m·K across its layers and 20 along them (round and along the can). 0.25 mm steel can, PVC wrap, 3 mm mandrel hole, 2.5 mm header under the + cap.

6 layers, 1.6 mm: 38 W/m·K in-plane and 0.45 through. The via zone under the stages conducts 8 W/m·K through. Parts are smeared into a board heat capacity of about 20 J/K. The P0 layout isn't final, so each port's stage is assumed to sit over its own front cell (USB1 over C4, USB2 over C1). The protection FETs are assumed at the bottom edge and the USB-C ports at the top.

BSC007N04LS6 2 × 0.85 mΩ, F102 2.5 mΩ, shunt 1 mΩ, nickel and copper 4.1 mΩ. SiZ240DT 13 mΩ at the 5 V gate drive (9 V drive off, as shipped). XGL7030-332 12 mΩ plus 0.15 W core at 500 kHz. 5 + 5 mΩ sense resistors, TPS25751 18 mΩ, USB-C 10 mΩ, 0.2 W per running converter.
MJF PA12 0.22 W/m·K (cup, cap, carrier), solid TPU bands 0.20, lattice bumpers 0.08. Air inside 0.038 W/m·K, which includes radiation across mm gaps.

The 10-21 policy in the spec, acting on the hottest of four NTCs. Each NTC is assumed at mid-length on the side of its can facing the pack centre. Board ramp 55 → 70 °C on each charger's TS NTC. 5 W re-advertising steps with 2 K hysteresis. USB1 priority with a 20 W USB2 minimum.
A generic silicon-graphite / NMC open-circuit curve, 3.5 V average, 6.5 Ah. Discharge stops at 2.8 V per cell under load. Charging stops at 95 %.
checks: Measure the 65E DC resistance with a 10 s pulse at 50 % and 10 % charge, and replace the 14 mΩ in pack3d.py.

Run 100 W from full with thermocouples on C4 at its board-facing stripe (z ≈ 40 mm), C4 at the NTC spot, C3, the USB1 FET case, the inductor and the outer face over the board. Compare the curves with this page. The stripe-to-NTC difference is the number that matters most.
Decide where the front-cell NTCs go. On the board-facing side, just above the filler (z ≈ 56 mm), they see the real hot spot. Then raise the derate start so the burst doesn't shrink.

Retune the discharge derate for the 65E. In the model a 40 → 44 °C cell ramp kept the cans under 48 °C and delivered 20 % more energy in the first 40 minutes. The 100 W burst itself sits right at the board ramp, so it only gets longer with a cooler stage or by splitting the load over both ports.
Cut a dummy module after dispensing to check the filler bead wets both the board and the cans across the whole zone.
method: The pack is a 100 × 87 × 64 voxel model (0.6 × 0.6 × 1.5 mm, about 480,000 cells inside the outline) built from the cup geometry in hardware/mechanical/monolith_shell.py and monolith_cup.py. Conductances between voxels come from a four-times-finer material grid. Thin layers like the cell wrap, the can and the 1.5 mm gaps between cells keep their real resistance. The wound cell roll is anisotropic, and the board is anisotropic with its via zone.

Time steps are implicit (10 s for discharge, 20 s for charging), solved with algebraic-multigrid CG. Each step runs the electrical model (loss per part, cell resistance by temperature and charge) and the firmware policy, then puts each loss into its part: the cell rolls, the nickel, the protection FETs, each stage's FETs, inductor, IC and sense resistors, each TPS25751 and each USB-C contact set.

Files: research_notes/Pack thermal BAK 65E/ in the repo. pack3d.py is the model and cases, fill.py the gap-filler options, sens.py the sensitivity runs, render.py the maps, summary.py the table. python jobs.py re-runs everything in about 1.5 h on 4 cores.
